system: You are an ambitious AI PhD student in computational genomics and functional genomics who is looking to publish a paper that will contribute significantly to the field.
task_description: You are given the following experiment that investigates whether late-layer embeddings from Evo2 — a DNA foundation model trained autoregressively on 8.8 trillion nucleotide tokens across all domains of life — encode functionally meaningful information about human genes. The baseline experiment fetches the promoter (2kb upstream of TSS) and coding sequence (CDS) for human genes in two functional classes: DNA repair genes (from KEGG pathways hsa03430/hsa03420/hsa03440/hsa03410) and tumor suppressor genes (curated from the Cancer Gene Census). It extracts mean-pooled late-layer (blocks.28.mlp.l3) embeddings from a frozen Evo2-7B model and compares four supervised probes: Logistic Regression (LR, linear), SVM-RBF (kernel nonlinear), XGBoost (tree-based nonlinear), and MLP (deep nonlinear). Baseline AUROCs: LR=0.66, SVM=0.72, XGBoost=?, MLP=0.74. The core research question is: which type of nonlinearity best captures functional information in Evo2 embeddings — kernel methods, tree ensembles, or deep networks? The most interesting experiments compare these model families: hyperparameter tuning for XGBoost (n_estimators, max_depth, learning_rate), XGBoost feature importance (which embedding dimensions matter most), model ensembling (combining XGBoost + MLP predictions), and calibration analysis. IMPORTANT CONSTRAINTS: (1) Do NOT add new gene classes or fetch additional genes — the dataset is already cached. (2) All experiments must reuse the cached dataset.json and embeddings_evo2_7b.npy files from run_0/data/. (3) Do NOT modify sequence inputs or embedding extraction — only modify analysis, clustering, and visualization code.
